pages.title: From signed contract to permission to operate

text.text: Most solar delays are paperwork, not roofs. The coordinator's job is to make sure no project waits on us, only on an office, and that every wait is visible.

Submit within five working days of the design being approved. The packet is the site plan, the panel layout with fire setbacks, the single-line diagram, the attachment spec and the structural letter if the roof needs one.
Make a row in Permits and utility approvals at
If the office sends corrections, move it to
and answer within two working days. The Lindgren-Baca project shows the cost of waiting: the install date has already passed.
when the permit is issued. Only then book the crew.
Homes in an association need the architecture committee's approval before the install, sometimes before the permit. Ask on the site survey. Committees meet monthly; a missed meeting costs four weeks.
, book the final inspection the same day. The inspector checks the attachments, the labels and placards, the rapid shutdown and the conduit. Keep the approved plan set in the garage for them.
The utility needs its own application, separate from the permit, and it only approves export once the inspection has passed. When the permission to operate letter arrives:
Call the homeowner and walk them through switching the system on and reading the monitoring app.
Check the first week's production against the estimate.
If a project waits on an office longer than its usual time, call them. A polite call moves more permits than a second email.

pages.title: Pricing a system and reading the margin

text.text: Price per watt is how homeowners compare quotes and how we check that a job is worth doing. This page explains the numbers on each project and the ranges we sell in.

Contract price divided by the system size in watts. An 8.4 kW system sold for 26,500 USD is 3.15 USD per watt. Our cash and loan price sits between 3.05 and 3.30 for panels only; tile roofs and long conduit runs sit at the top of that range.

A battery adds about 12,000 to 14,000 USD to the contract and lowers the margin percentage, because the battery itself is most of the cost. Sell it for what it does, backup during outages and storing midday power for the evening, not as a profit line.
panels, inverters, racking, wire, and the battery if there is one. Pull them from Equipment stock and reorder anything that drops to its reorder point.
crew hours at their loaded rate, plus the electrician's day for the panel work.
building permit, plan review and any utility study fee.
Begay and Okwuosa show the battery pattern: higher contracts, lower percentages, and still worth doing.

Estimated production is System size times the project's Production factor: the kWh one installed kW makes in a year on that roof. New projects start at 1,450, a middle figure; set it from your design tool's estimate for the roof, about 1,600 for an open south roof in a sunny state and 1,100 to 1,300 for shade or a cloudy region.

compares that with the household's last twelve months. Size to 90% to 105%. Oversizing sells more panels but leaves the homeowner exporting power at a low credit, and that shows up in reviews a year later.
A signed contract can be cancelled during the legal cooling-off period. Mark the project Cancelled; margin leaves its numbers blank so the dashboard stays honest.
Crews, roofs and inspections for the next six weeks. A project is only scheduled once its permit is approved and the equipment is in the warehouse.
A good survey is the difference between the system we sold and the one we can build. Measure once, photograph everything, and set the production factor from what you saw.
Pull the last twelve months of usage from the homeowner's bill and write the yearly kWh on the homeowner.
Look at the roof on satellite: direction, pitch, trees, vents and skylights.
Measure each usable face and note the direction it faces.
Check roof age and condition. Over 15 years on composition shingle, quote the reroof first.
Find the rafters and their spacing; note the attic access.
Read shading at three times of day with your app, or by eye at noon and late afternoon.
Photograph the panel label, the main breaker and any open slots.
A 100 amp panel with a battery usually needs a panel upgrade; price it now.
